_comment: The Security 101 study edition — Microsoft's 'Cybersecurity for Beginners' (Security-101) digested for study. Original curriculum (c) Microsoft, MIT License, github.com/microsoft/Security-101. Keys are QALAM-authored study points: the compressed layer, the mnemonics, the things worth carrying into the exam room. Lesson links point into the QALAM fork.

modules.title: Basic security concepts
modules.blurb: The vocabulary everything else is written in: the triad, the threats, the risk, the paperwork, and the two models that re-drew the map.

lessons.title: The CIA triad and other key concepts
lessons.objective: Confidentiality, availability and integrity — plus authenticity, nonrepudiation and privacy.
keys: Confidentiality — only authorized eyes see it; broken by disclosure: leaks, eavesdropping, misdirected access
Integrity — data stays correct and unaltered; broken by tampering, in transit or at rest
Availability — the right people can use it when they need it; broken by outage, DoS, destruction
Authenticity + nonrepudiation — claims are true and can't credibly be denied later
Privacy spans all three — the data subject keeps control of their own information

lessons.title: Common cybersecurity threats
lessons.objective: The threat landscape facing individuals and organizations.
keys: Threat = potential harm · vulnerability = the weakness · exploit = the tool that joins them
Malware families: virus (attaches), worm (self-spreads), ransomware (denies + extorts), spyware (watches)
Social engineering beats firewalls — phishing, spear-phishing, business email compromise target people
Insider threat needs no exploit: authorized access, unauthorized intent
Attack surface = every point a threat can touch — people, process and technology

lessons.title: Understanding risk management
lessons.objective: Assessing risk — impact and likelihood — and implementing controls.
keys: Risk = likelihood × impact — it is managed, never eliminated
Four responses: avoid, mitigate (controls), transfer (insurance/provider), accept (documented!)
Controls: physical / technical / administrative — and preventive / detective / corrective
The risk register is a living document — unreviewed risk data is fiction

lessons.title: Security practices and documentation
lessons.objective: The difference between policies, procedures, standards and regulations.
keys: Policy = intent (what and why) · standard = the mandatory specific · procedure = the step-by-step how
Regulations and law are external and non-negotiable; policy is yours to write
Documentation is itself a control — unwritten security is unauditable security

lessons.title: Zero trust
lessons.objective: What zero trust is, defense in depth, and the architecture it forces.
keys: Never trust, always verify — network location grants nothing
Assume breach — design as if the attacker is already inside
Defense in depth — layered controls so one failure is never the whole story
Every request answers: who/what is asking, for which data, under which conditions

lessons.title: The shared responsibility model
lessons.objective: Who secures what in the cloud — and why the boundary moves.
keys: Provider secures the fabric (the cloud); you secure what you put on it (in the cloud)
On-prem = you own everything · SaaS = mostly provider · IaaS/PaaS = split
The split is documented by the provider — read it before you assume it

lessons.title: End of module quiz
lessons.objective: Prove module 1 stuck.

modules.title: Identity & access management
modules.blurb: The new perimeter: who you are, what you may do, and how little access is enough.

lessons.title: IAM key concepts
lessons.objective: Least privilege, segregation of duties, and how IAM supports zero trust.
keys: The four steps: identify (claim) → authenticate (prove) → authorize (allow) → account (log)
Least privilege: minimum access, for the minimum time
Segregation of duties — no single person completes a critical flow alone
AAA is the spine: authentication, authorization, accounting

lessons.title: IAM zero trust architecture
lessons.objective: Identity as the new perimeter, and the threats that mitigates.
keys: Identity is the new perimeter — the network edge no longer decides access
Strong auth: MFA everywhere; passwordless where possible
Conditional access weighs signals per request — device, location, risk
What it neutralizes: credential theft, lateral movement, privilege creep

lessons.title: IAM capabilities
lessons.objective: The capabilities and controls that secure identities.
keys: One directory / identity provider is the source of truth (Entra ID and friends)
SSO = one identity, many apps; federation extends trust across organizations
Privileged access: just-in-time, approved, logged, revoked
Lifecycle automation (joiner-mover-leaver) kills orphan accounts

lessons.title: End of module quiz
lessons.objective: Prove module 2 stuck.

modules.title: Network security
modules.blurb: The roads the data travels — and the checkpoints zero trust puts on them.

lessons.title: Networking key concepts
lessons.objective: IP addressing, port numbers, encryption and friends.
keys: IP address = where; port = which door — know the famous ones (80/443, 22, 53)
TCP guarantees delivery, UDP prefers speed — services pick their poison
TLS protects the conversation in transit — not the endpoints themselves
DNS, DHCP, NAT — the plumbing, and the plumbing attackers also love

lessons.title: Networking zero trust architecture
lessons.objective: Networking's role in end-to-end zero trust.
keys: Micro-segmentation — tiny blast radii, explicitly allowed flows only
The network sits inside identity now: per-request access, not per-subnet
Encrypt east-west too — internal traffic is not 'safe' by location

lessons.title: Network security capabilities
lessons.objective: The tooling — firewalls, WAF, DDoS protection and the rest.
keys: Firewall filters L3/L4; WAF defends L7 — the app attacks: SQLi, XSS
DDoS protection absorbs volume — CDN edges and scrubbing centers
IDS notices, IPS acts; modern NDR watches behaviour, not signatures
A VPN grants access, not safety — zero trust retires the implicit tunnel

lessons.title: End of module quiz
lessons.objective: Prove module 3 stuck.

modules.title: Security operations
modules.blurb: The defenders' shift: detect, respond, recover — and hunt instead of wait.

lessons.title: SecOps key concepts
lessons.objective: Why SecOps exists, and how it differs from IT operations.
keys: SecOps fuses security with IT ops: detect, respond, recover, learn
Different instinct from ops: adversary thinking, not just uptime thinking
The metrics that matter: MTTD and MTTR — time to find, time to fix

lessons.title: SecOps zero trust architecture
lessons.objective: How SecOps contributes to end-to-end zero trust.
keys: Telemetry everywhere — you cannot respond to what you never saw
The SIEM is SecOps memory: central logs, correlated
Assume compromise → hunt proactively; alerts are the floor, not the ceiling

lessons.title: SecOps capabilities
lessons.objective: The tooling — SIEM, XDR and beyond.
keys: SIEM collects, correlates, alerts; XDR extends to endpoint, identity, email
SOAR runs the playbook — automation takes the repetitive triage
A SOC tiers up: triage → investigation → threat hunting

lessons.title: End of module quiz
lessons.objective: Prove module 4 stuck.

modules.title: Application security
modules.blurb: Where code meets attacker: build it right, then prove it stays right.

lessons.title: AppSec key concepts
lessons.objective: Secure by design, input validation and friends.
keys: Secure by design beats patching later — security rides in the requirements
Never trust input: validate, sanitize, encode — at every boundary
The OWASP Top 10 is the checklist of the usual app wounds
Least privilege applies to code too — and to its dependencies

lessons.title: AppSec key capabilities
lessons.objective: Pipeline security tools — code scanning, secret scanning and friends.
keys: SAST reads the code · DAST attacks the running app · SCA watches dependencies
Secret scanning: keys never belong in a repo — not even one commit
Shift left: the pipeline is the cheapest place to find and fix

lessons.title: End of module quiz
lessons.objective: Prove module 5 stuck.

modules.title: Infrastructure security
modules.blurb: The ground floor: hardened systems, patched holes, contained containers.

lessons.title: Infrastructure security key concepts
lessons.objective: Hardening, patching, security hygiene, container security.
keys: Hardening = removing the unnecessary — ports, services, default accounts
Patch discipline: known unpatched CVEs remain the most common way in
Containers inherit the host's sins — patch the base image, not just the app
Hygiene: tested backups, least-privilege service accounts

lessons.title: Infrastructure security capabilities
lessons.objective: Tooling that assists — CSPM, container security and friends.
keys: CSPM watches cloud posture against benchmarks (CIS)
Image scanning belongs in the registry and the pipeline
IaC scanning catches the misconfiguration before it ever deploys

lessons.title: End of module quiz
lessons.objective: Prove module 6 stuck.

modules.title: Data security
modules.blurb: What it's all for: the data — classified, retained, watched, governed.

lessons.title: Data security key concepts
lessons.objective: Classification and retention, and why they matter.
keys: Classification drives handling — you cannot protect what you haven't labelled
Retention: keep only what's needed; scheduled deletion is a control
Three states, three duties: at rest, in transit, in use — encrypt accordingly

lessons.title: Data security capabilities
lessons.objective: DLP, insider risk management, data governance.
keys: DLP watches and blocks the exits — email, USB, upload
Insider risk: watch the patterns, respect privacy and the law
Governance names owners — who holds which data, who may decide

lessons.title: End of module quiz
lessons.objective: Prove module 7 stuck.

modules.title: AI security
modules.blurb: The new frontier: models that inherit every old risk and invent new ones.

lessons.title: AI security key concepts
lessons.objective: Traditional security vs AI security — the differences and similarities.
keys: AI inherits the old risks (access, supply chain) and adds new ones (model, prompt)
The model is code + data — both are attack surfaces
Adversarial inputs target behaviour, not just availability

lessons.title: AI security capabilities
lessons.objective: The tooling and controls that secure AI.
keys: Content filtering + grounding tame hallucination and injection harm
Log prompts and outputs — that's the forensic trail for AI incidents
Red-team the model like any other boundary

lessons.title: Responsible AI
lessons.objective: What responsible AI is, and the AI-specific harms to know.
keys: Fairness, privacy, transparency, accountability — design constraints, not afterthoughts
The harms to know: bias, misuse, overreliance, sensitive-data disclosure
Human oversight stays where the stakes are high
